units.translation: Thus M. Wieseler seems rightly to read καὶ τῷ μὲν εἰ σὺ κάρτ᾽ ἐμοῦ σοφωτέρα [and in that respect, if you are far wiser than I], which the scholiast seems to have read, who explains it as διὰ τὸν χρόνον [because of the time].
And yet what do I say?
And yet who else but I fully assigned these honors to the younger gods?
And yet even as I speak, I lament.
I will share my anger with you; for you are older. And yet you are far wiser than I.
and in that respect, if you are far wiser than I
with a tongue that announces evil
you have poured out a lifeless cowardice
faulty for κάκκυνηγετῶ or καὶ κυνηγετῶ. See κυνηγετέω.
faulty for κάκκυνηγετῶ [I hunt badly] or καὶ κυνηγετῶ [and I hunt]. See κυνηγετέω [to hunt].
and the prophetess, the Erinys invoked by my father
my heart, a prophet of evil, is greatly troubled within

Scholiast: θρήνον ἀμελή καὶ ἄμουσον, κακὸν καὶ ἄμουσον μέλος ἔχουσαν, ὡς θρηνώδη καὶ ἀπευκτήν. ήν [a neglected and unmusical lament, having an evil and unmusical song, as mournful and abominable]. Heath rightly says: "A word occupied with uttering evils: from μέλομαι [to be an object of care], not from μέλος [song], from which no analogy can be derived." Less aptly Paleius says 'meditating evils.'
a neglected and unmusical lament, having an evil and unmusical song, as mournful and abominable
to be an object of care
From where do you have the bounds of your divine path, speaking evil?
As a substantive, κακόν or with the article τὸ κακόν, evil; it is said of any evil that someone either suffers or does.
i.e. an evil gift of evils upon evils, with which Linwood compares Soph. Ai.853 πόνος πόνῳ πόνον φέρει [toil brings toil upon toil].
as Ch. 123 τὸν ἐχθρὸν ἀνταμείβεσθαι κακοῖς [to repay the enemy with evils].
about death, and likewise 301 θάνατον ὅσπερ μέγιστον ῥῦμα τῶν πολλῶν κακῶν [death, which is the greatest deliverance from many evils].
which fragment seems rightly to be attributed to Euripides by Stobaeus 108, 43.
he does not like to be bad
there is nothing worse than bad company
cast out the beginning of evil desire
you will not be called bad
yet the god honors even a bad victory
a cold evil falls upon my heart
if the Greeks should escape an evil fate
these things (more probably ταὐτά τοι [these very things]) bold Xerxes learns by associating with evil men
an evil gift of evils to evil men
in the manner of bad bronze
by the twisting of a bad shepherd
the evil of wealth in clothing
to fawn upon a bad man
even a bad prophet would know these things
an enemy, as it seems, an evil one
rightly assigning unjust things to the evil, and holy things to the lawful
he bears an evil, ready tongue
